hook: By the 1940s, twenty or thirty remained. The largest cat came back.

story.text: The Amur tiger is the largest cat alive: up to ten feet nose to tail, six hundred and sixty pounds, moving soundlessly on fur-lined paws.
It is the only tiger built for deep winter — the thickest coat of any tiger, a short ruff, snow-pale orange with sparse stripes.
Its forest runs on one tree: Korean pine, whose nuts feed the boar and deer that feed the tiger.
A single tiger may range over ten thousand square kilometers.
In the early 1900s hunters took fifty or sixty tigers a year, until by the 1940s only twenty or thirty were thought to remain.
Russia's 1948 hunting ban — the first tiger protection of its kind — likely saved the subspecies.
Recovery has been slow and guarded: rangers backed with intelligence support, and camera traps watching the same valleys since 1992.
Even orphans count: six rescued cubs released in the Pri-Amur have produced at least twelve wild cubs where tigers were absent for fifty years.
Russia's 2022 census counted more than 750, and across the Chinese border sightings keep increasing.
To witness the Amur tiger is to stand with the deep snow forests — and against everything the poachers' market still wants from them.

reproduction.text: Two to four cubs are typical, born after about a hundred days and staying with their mother up to two years. Usually only two survive — and each will one day need an enormous territory of its own.

insight.text: A single Amur tiger's range can exceed 10,000 square kilometers — and for all that size, it can clear roughly eighteen feet in one jump.
